title: World Cup final tickets go on sale for more than $2.2million each
content:
Four tickets for this summer’s World Cup final in the U.S. have gone on sale for more than $2million each.

FIFA’s official “resale/exchange marketplace” website lists the quartet of Category 1 seats for the match at the MetLife Stadium, New Jersey, on July 19 for $2,299,998.85 (£1.7m) each, according to Sky News.

Other tickets in the same category and section, behind one of the goals at the 82,500-capacity arena, can be purchased for $16,098 (£11,953).

FIFA, the sport’s global governing body, does not control the price of tickets listed for resale — which is legal under U.S. and Canadian law — but takes a 15 per cent cut from both buyer and seller, which is included in the overall price. FIFA would, in theory, therefore pocket $600,000 if just one of the four tickets is sold.

Tickets listed for resale at previous tournaments have been capped at face value.

Tickets for resale in the U.S. and Canada are listed on the same website, while matches in Mexico operate on a separate platform where tickets can only be listed at face value or lower for Mexican citizens, with no premium pricing allowed.

FIFA has faced fierce criticism for ticket prices at the tournament, which will be be jointly-hosted by the U.S., Canada and Mexico from June 11.

The Athletic reporting on April 1 that fans were left frustrated by long waits, technical glitches and hiked prices when the final phase of sales opened.

On April 9, The Athletic reported that FIFA had introduced a new category of tickets — “Front Category 1” — in an apparently attempt to milk more money from prime seats.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino admitted last week that he “didn’t know” prior to the start of the process that reselling tickets was legal in the U.S. — albeit regulated by state law — and defended prices, citing a “very special market”. Infantino also reiterated that FIFA is a non-profit organisation.

“What many people don’t know, because of course we generate billions in a World Cup, people don’t know FIFA is a non-for profit organisation, which means all the revenue we generate, we invest them in the organisation of the game, in 211 countries all over the world,” Infantino said at an event organised by Semafor. “Three-quarters of which probably would not be able to have organised football without the grants we could give them, so we always try to find the right balance.”

A FIFA spokesperson told The Athletic: “FIFA has established a ticket sales and secondary market model that reflects standard ticket market practices for major sporting and entertainment events across the host countries.

“The applicable resale facilitation fees are aligned with industry standards across North American sports and entertainment sectors.

“FIFA’s variable pricing ticketing approach aligns with industry trends across various sports and entertainment sectors, where price adaptations are made to optimise sales and attendance and ensure a fair market value for events.”
